title: dual-nonlinear-glu: revisiting the linear value branch of gated layers
description:
Gated layers in transformers keep their value branch linear: SwiGLU is silu(W_g h) * (W_u h). Making both branches nonlinear is not a new design — it is the Gated Tanh Unit, which Dauphin et al. (2017) measured and rejected because both branches contribute a gradient downscaling factor, and the GLU → GEGLU → SwiGLU line descends from that rejection. On a synthetic teacher–student benchmark with a residual and a 1/sqrt(depth) branch initialisation, that rejection does not reproduce.

The larger finding is about a different property. The proposed pair f and g, like max(ax,-b) and the identity, are all linear above zero, and it is that linear positive half which costs. Removing it from the gate — a plain b·tanh(a x/b) on both sides — is worth 1.5–5.9× in all four cells of two teachers by two value branches; removing it from the value branch is 1.0–3.0×, with one cell where it does nothing. The two changes are redundant rather than additive. This is the one effect that two teachers giving otherwise opposite accounts both support.

A control separates the mechanism. A fixed tanh, with nothing learned, keeps most of the gain when the value branch is nonlinear but falls below SwiGLU when it is not, because it sits in its own linear region (median argument 0.378) while a learned gate drives itself into saturation (median 3.2). What the learned scale buys is the operating point, and that decides the outcome only when the gate is the sole nonlinearity. The saturated gate is not a sign function — that was tested and is wrong, at 3.70× — but a clamp costs only 1.19×, and training with the clamp from the start costs 9%, so the gate needs no transcendental at all.

Also recorded. asinh in the value branch can be evaluated by polynomials alone, with segment boundaries taken from the measured argument distribution rather than from the shape of asinh, reproducing a trained network's loss to seven figures and costing 30× on a GPU, where it must not be used; the block's output is the mixed second derivative of an elementary potential F(u)G(v), which survives the both-sides form; initialising the residual branch at 1/sqrt(depth) outweighs every activation choice measured; curvature-aware ternary rounding was derived, corrected, and failed; and a benchmark checklist for detecting tasks that do not need depth.

Corrections to v0.1.0 are recorded in place: two measured statements about GPU kernel cost, an inference-time substitution described as free that costs 4.4%, and a 2.1× gain attributed to the wrong one of two simultaneous changes.
